pairs.question: Why do you want to work at [company]?
pairs.answer: I've spent the last 5 years building high-performance, multi-platform consumer experiences at Amazon Fire TV (200M+ devices) and Best Buy. What draws me to [company] specifically is [research the company -- mission, product, stage]. My experience shipping across Android native (Kotlin/Compose), React Native, and backend services maps directly to the full-stack nature of the work, and I'm most productive when I can own a feature end-to-end rather than working in one narrow layer.

pairs.question: What is the most impressive project you've worked on? Why is it impressive?
pairs.answer: The Fire TV Burton navigation architecture -- a complete reimagining of how 200M+ Fire TV devices render their home screen. I designed and shipped a system where all navigation tabs stay live simultaneously as ViewModelContainers, with distance-ordered background preloading and a Compose-based precomposer that keeps bitmaps resident for only the nearest 3 tabs. A 7-tier device-eligibility rollout system let us ship two completely different UI architectures in the same APK with zero downtime. The crash rate on the navigation path dropped 73% and tab-switch latency improved 28%.

pairs.question: Tell us about a time you built a feature for users who weren't engineers (analysts, coaches, operations staff, etc.). How did you figure out what they actually needed, and how did that shape your technical approach?
pairs.answer:
At Amazon Fire TV, I built internal diagnostic and device-state tooling for operations and QA teams. They were manually cross-referencing 3 dashboards and a spreadsheet to answer 'why does this device show a different home screen?'

I sat in on their triage calls. The real need wasn't 'a better dashboard' -- it was a single answer to 'what is this device running and why?'

I built a device-state lookup tool that took a DSN, queried the 7-tier eligibility resolution system I'd designed, and returned a plain-English breakdown. The backend queried the same eligibility code the launcher uses (ground truth). The frontend was a simple React form -- paste a DSN, get the answer. I showed only the winning tier, with a collapsible 'full chain' for the curious.

pairs.question: Walk us through a full-stack feature you owned end to end, from planning through release and support.
pairs.answer: The 'Offers for You' personalized recommendation slider at Best Buy Mobile. Backend: GraphQL endpoint returning ranked product cards with pricing, badge logic, and deep-link URLs. Frontend: React Native horizontal ScrollView with lazy-loaded cards, impression tracking (50%+ visibility for 1+ second), and prefetched images for the first 5 cards. Chose ScrollView over FlatList because the set was capped at 20 items. Feature flag, 10% -> 50% -> 100% rollout. 17% MAU engagement uplift. Added a lightweight price-check on render for visible cards to fix stale-pricing complaints.

pairs.question: Describe a tricky bug or production issue you tracked down. How did you find the root cause?
pairs.answer: A production crash on Fire TV affecting 60K+ occurrences across 11 hardware targets. NPE in LayoutNodeDrawScope.drawContent() attributed to ImageCache$1. Decompiled the debug APK's smali and confirmed R8 had horizontally merged an unrelated lambda into ImageCache$1's class slot. The real origin was a GraphicsLayer recording from a draw-modifier node mid-attach/detach. Root cause: a @Composable modifier with an early 'return this' before remember/DisposableEffect calls, causing slot table desynchronization. Fix: restored composed{}. Added slot-stability test, CI audit for conditional returns before slot-producing calls, and 'verify crash branch matches crashing build' as mandatory RCA step. Crash rate dropped 73%.

pairs.question: What interests you about building internal platforms?
pairs.answer: The leverage and feedback loop. At Amazon Fire TV, I replaced a manual 3-dashboard cross-referencing workflow with a single lookup tool. Operations staff stopped escalating questions to engineering. Internal platforms have a uniquely fast feedback loop: ship Tuesday, watch people use it Wednesday, fix Thursday. Building for Operations, Support, Marketing, and Risk teams forces discipline about API design, permissions, and progressive disclosure -- a harder design problem than most consumer products.

pairs.question: What's the most interesting technology you've discovered recently? How does it work?
pairs.answer: I built a fully automated job scanning pipeline using an autonomous agent management layer (Kiro Crew). It runs as a macOS LaunchAgent daemon, hourly fetching listings from multiple job boards, scoring them against my resume using embedding-based pre-filtering plus LLM evaluation, auto-generating tailored resumes, and delivering matches via iMessage. Circuit breaker state machines per data source prevent cascading failures. Two-layer relevance filtering -- fast regex cuts 84% of junk, LLM catches edge cases. Outcome-calibrated scoring from real application history. Survives sleep/crashes/reboots via launchd.

pairs.question: Please share your proudest Android feature in 2-3 sentences. What made it challenging and what was the impact?
pairs.answer: The Burton navigation architecture on Fire TV -- a Jetpack Compose system where all home screen tabs stay live simultaneously with distance-ordered background preloading and a compositor that keeps bitmaps resident for only the nearest 3 tabs. The challenge was making sub-frame tab switches work reliably across 11 hardware targets within a shared 26MB image budget, while shipping two different UI architectures in one APK via a 7-tier remote config rollout. It reduced tab-switch latency by 28% and dropped navigation crash rates 73% across 200M+ devices.

pairs.question: Have you contributed to a mobile app(s) and/or several features that reached a large number of users? Please describe.
pairs.answer: Yes -- the Amazon Fire TV Launcher ships to 200M+ registered devices globally. I've owned features across the full home screen: the Burton navigation system, personalized content recommendation carousels, device-eligibility rollout architecture, and VoiceView accessibility improvements. Before that, I built 12 user-facing features in the Best Buy mobile app (React Native, millions of MAU), including the 'Offers for You' personalized recommendation slider that drove a 17% uplift in monthly active engagement.

Describe a bug or problem that took you much longer than expected to solve. What was actually going on and how did you figure it out?
pairs.answer: A production crash on Fire TV affecting 60K+ occurrences across 11 hardware targets -- an NPE in LayoutNodeDrawScope.drawContent() that the stack trace attributed to ImageCache$1. I spent days investigating ImageCache before realizing R8 had horizontally merged a completely unrelated lambda into that class slot. I confirmed it by decompiling the debug APK's smali and matching the class shape against the crash frame's method signature. The real origin was a @Composable modifier with a conditional early return that desynchronized Compose's slot table, tearing draw-modifier coordinator chains during recomposition. What made it take so long: I initially investigated the wrong branch (mainline instead of the hotfix branch the crashing build was actually cut from), and the R8 relabeling meant the stack trace was literally pointing at the wrong class.

pairs.question: Tell us about something you built that nobody required you to build. What was it and why did you build it?
pairs.answer: An autonomous job scanning pipeline. I was applying to dozens of roles and spending hours on mechanical work -- searching boards, reading JDs, retyping the same answers. So I built a system that runs as a macOS LaunchAgent daemon, hourly scraping Greenhouse/Lever/Ashby career pages, scoring roles against my resume with a two-layer filter (regex pre-filter cuts 84% of junk, then LLM evaluation for career-trajectory fit), auto-generating tailored resumes, and delivering matches via iMessage with the PDF attached. I also built Filli -- a browser extension that auto-fills job application forms from saved answers -- because I was still retyping the same application answers on every form. Nobody asked for either. I built them because the problem was repetitive and solvable.

pairs.question: What part of this role do you expect to be your steepest learning curve and why?
pairs.answer: The domain-specific context. I can ship Android features, debug production crashes, and build backend services -- that transfers anywhere. What doesn't transfer is understanding how this company's product actually works for its users, what the existing codebase's unwritten assumptions are, and which past architectural decisions constrain what's possible now. Every codebase has a history that isn't in the docs. That's the part that takes time and can't be shortcut -- you have to read the code, ask questions, and ship a few features before you really understand the system.
